nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What is highlighted as a significant concern for industries affected by Natural Hazards Triggering Technological Accidents (Natech)?
nodes.answer: The risk of the release of POPs and other PBTs by these industries should be globally evaluated.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Background Large quantities of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and other persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic sub - stances (PBTs) like heavy metals have accumulated mainly over the last century in reservoirs, such as landfills, dump sites, contaminated sites, and mine tailings, as well as in environmental sinks like soils and sediments. Large floods in the past 20 years have demonstrated the mobilisation of POPs/PBTs from these reservoirs, underscoring the limitations of conven- tional technical safeguard measures like leachate and wastewater treatment or containment systems at landfills. Results This study emphasises the need to develop inventories of POPs/PBTs in these reservoirs for the assessment of future risk of increased flooding triggered by climate change and for priority setting of remediation and securing measures. Further, sea-level rise should be included in these assessments as long-term risk for large areas that are likely to be permanently flooded in the coming decades and centuries. In addition, the risk of release of POPs and other PBTs by industries affected by Natural Hazards Triggering Technological Accidents (Natech) should be globally evaluated. The review emphasises the importance of conducting systematic assessments and inventories to understand the risk of these reservoirs for environmental pollution and human exposure.

nodes.question: What type of data is required during the nuclear reactor approval process?
nodes.answer: The approval process requires data collected on reactor materials and parts both pre-and post-irradiation and under various extreme environments.
nodes.paragraph: This work describes the X- ray computed tomography post-irradiation examination capabilities at INL, aswell as detailing a variety of applications this instrument has examined. INTRODUCTION As international industrialization and worldwide population growth continue to occur, future energydemands are projected to increase by approximately 30% by the year 2050. 1According to the Interna- tional Energy Agency S World Energy Outlook2023,2the development and implementation of affordable, clean energy options is imperative to reaching the 1.5 /C176C limit on global warming by 2050 as established by the Paris Agreement.3Fortu- nately, nuclear energy is an attractive sector of the world S future energy portfolio as it is a power-dense energy source capable of producing energy at largescale while being carbon-free and virtually emis- sion-free.4Nuclear energy S ability to provide a consistent, continuous baseload energy with sched-uled downtime occurring only every /C2418 24 months (or longer, depending on reactor type) for refueling makes it a more competitive optionthan some other green energy sources. Before new nuclear reactor concepts can be commercially implemented in the United States, they must be approved for licensing by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission. 5The approval process requires a plethora of data, including datacollected on reactor materials and parts both pre-and post-irradiation and under a variety of extreme environments to ensure safe operations.

nodes.question: What kind of facility is the Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL)?
nodes.answer: IMCL is a Hazard Category-2 Nuclear Facility that can handle highly radioactive materials.
nodes.paragraph: 39The goal of introducing XCT into the PIE work ow for nuclear materials is twofold. First, XCT provides a non-destructive means to probe the structure inthree dimensions, providing the potential to revealinvaluable insights into the effects of irradiation on the evolution of material structures. 40Second, XCT can inform subsequent targeted destructive analy-sis by identifying features of interest for further examination with higher-resolution, smaller eld- of-view (FOV) techniques without having to ran-domly search for desired features, saving time and improving results. The larger FOV of XCT also ensures a region of interest (ROI) is representativeof the larger sample composition. Additionally, realistic internal 3D geometry generated using XCT can be meshed and used as a high- delityinput for fuel performance and other modelingefforts. This paper describes the XCT capabilities at INL and its application to support INL S mission of examining energy materials with an emphasis onPIE capabilities. INSTRUMENTATION AND FACILITY INFORMATION Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory (IMCL) Facility IMCL, which began operations in 2015, 41is a Hazard Category-2 Nuclear Facility that can handle highly radioactive materials. It consists of a varietyof tools to enable PIE of irradiated materials forcharacterization of material performance inChuirazzi, Kancharla, and Morankar 1338 extreme reactor environments which contain high temperatures and large radiation elds.

nodes.question: What was the order of samples used for testing and commissioning the instrument?
nodes.answer: The order was nonradioactive samples, unirradiated nuclear fuel, irradiated non-fuel samples, and finally irradiated nuclear fuel samples by the end of 2021.
nodes.paragraph: Initially, nonradioactive samples were used to test and commission the instrument as a graded approach towards radiation work. After initialcommissioning efforts, unirradiated nuclear fuel was examined, then irradiated non-fuel samples, before nally performing XCT on irradiated nuclearfuel samples by the end of 2021. The system ismaintained as a clean environment, meaning it is not contaminated and samples can be introduced and released from the system without becomingradiologically contaminated. This is achieved by fully encapsulating contaminated or radioactive samples to prevent them from contaminating eXRM S cabinet. The Xradia 520 is equipped with both a at panel detector and an X-ray microscope. The at paneldetector provides a larger FOV (maximum of30.7 cm 919.4 cm) with spatial resolution of the images ranging from /C246Im/pixel up to 100 Im/ pixel. Spatial resolution is reported as the distanceof an isotropic pixel edge length in a 2D image (a voxel in a reconstructed 3D tomogram). The XRM also contains a set of objective lenses, each directlycoated with X-ray scintillators, that are optically coupled to an Andor iKon-L charge-coupled device (CCD) camera. These objective lenses provide asmaller FOV than the at panel detector (minimum of 0.6 mm 90.6 mm) but a much higher spatial resolution ranging from /C24250 nm/pixel to 55 Im/ pixel.

nodes.question: What are some common effects of gamma irradiation on chromosomal activity?
nodes.answer: Gamma irradiation disturbs mitotic activity, induces chromosomal aberration, and affects yield, with common changes including stickiness, lagging chromosomes, and bridges at anaphase and telophase.
nodes.paragraph: In addition, gamma rays are essential physical activators for crop plant growth, yield attributes, and yields without using external fertilizers. The use of low doses of gamma irradiation in combination with drought stress displays better performance than that of the non-irradiated plants under the same condition [14]. A cytogenetic analysis is important in assessing genetic impact of the chemical and physical mutagens [15]. These changes provide the basis for introducing genetic variability in many plant traits [16]. The most common influence of -irradiation is disturbing mitotic activity inducing chromosomal aberration, and affecting yield. The most common chromosomal changes recorded in response to -irradiation is the production of mitotic chromosomal aberrations; stickiness, lagging chromo - somes and bridges at anaphase and telophase [17]. How - ever, the only recoverable chromosomal rearrangements are those that can replicate DNA molecules and hence can be stably passed on to the next generation [18]. Sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electropho - resis (SDS-PAGE) of storage seed protein was used to differentiate between cultivars of Zea mays and to iden - tify inbred lines [19].
